_comment: Prayer levels 16-18: pastoral difficulties and doubts (remapped old L7), the Examen as a further daily habit, the Trinity/kataphatic-apophatic/guides for prayer (remapped old L8)

questions.prompt: Someone says, 'I used to feel close to God when I prayed, but now prayer just feels dry and empty -- I think it doesn't work anymore.' Per CCC 2727-2733, what is the more accurate way to understand this experience?
choices: This sounds like spiritual dryness, a real and common experience in the life of prayer that is not the same as prayer failing or God being absent
This proves the person has committed a serious sin that has cut them off from God entirely
This means the person should stop praying until the feeling returns on its own
This is proof that prayer has no real spiritual effect and never did
questions.correctAnswer: This sounds like spiritual dryness, a real and common experience in the life of prayer that is not the same as prayer failing or God being absent
questions.explanation: CCC 2731 names dryness as a real, common trial in prayer, distinct from distraction (the mind simply wandering) -- it is not evidence God has withdrawn or that prayer has stopped 'working,' but a real experience the saints themselves describe encountering, which faithfulness through rather than abandonment of prayer is the traditional response to.
questions.hint: The Catechism has a specific name for this exact experience, distinct from ordinary distraction.

citations.quote: Dryness belongs to contemplative prayer when the heart is separated from God, with no taste for thoughts, memories, and feelings, even spiritual ones. This is the moment of sheer faith clinging faithfully to Jesus in his agony and in his tomb.

questions.prompt: An objector cites Matthew 6:7 ('do not babble like the pagans... they think they will be heard because of their many words') to argue the Rosary is 'vain repetition.' Using CCC 2668, what is the accurate response?
choices: Matthew 6:7 condemns empty, faithless babbling meant to manipulate God with sheer word-count, not repeated prayer offered with attention and love, which the Church distinguishes as a different thing entirely
The Church agrees the Rosary is exactly the practice Matthew 6:7 condemns
Matthew 6:7 has been formally removed from the Catholic canon of Scripture
Repetition of any kind in prayer has never been practiced by any saint
questions.correctAnswer: Matthew 6:7 condemns empty, faithless babbling meant to manipulate God with sheer word-count, not repeated prayer offered with attention and love, which the Church distinguishes as a different thing entirely
questions.explanation: CCC 2668 situates repeated invocation (like the Jesus Prayer, and by extension the Rosary's repeated Hail Marys) as a form of continual prayer rooted in attention and love, not the manipulative, faithless 'babbling' Matthew 6:7 actually condemns -- the target of Jesus's warning is the attitude behind the words, not repetition itself.
questions.hint: The key distinction is the attitude behind the words -- manipulative word-count versus attentive, loving repetition.

citations.quote: In praying, do not babble like the pagans, who think that they will be heard because of their many words.

The invocation of the holy name of Jesus is the simplest way of praying always... the prayer is not lost by heaping up empty phrases, but holds fast to the word and 'brings forth fruit with patience.'

questions.prompt: A child asks, 'If God already knows what I need, why do I have to ask for it in prayer?' Applying CCC 2736's answer, what is the most accurate response?
choices: Asking in prayer is part of how God has willed to draw us into a real relationship of trust and dependence on Him, not information He is otherwise missing
God does not actually know what we need until we tell Him in prayer
Petitionary prayer is only a formality with no real spiritual purpose
Asking for things is discouraged in Catholic prayer; only adoration is truly valid
questions.correctAnswer: Asking in prayer is part of how God has willed to draw us into a real relationship of trust and dependence on Him, not information He is otherwise missing
questions.explanation: CCC 2736 teaches that petitionary prayer isn't supplying God with information He lacks -- it's part of the real, willed relationship of a child asking a Father, deepening trust and dependence rather than serving a merely informational function.
questions.hint: The point of asking isn't to inform God -- it's about the relationship the asking itself expresses and deepens.

citations.quote: Are we convinced that 'we do not know how to pray as we ought'? Our Father knows what we need before we ask him, but he awaits our petition because the dignity of his children lies in their freedom.

questions.prompt: Why does the Our Father open with 'hallowed be thy name' and 'thy kingdom come' before any petition for daily needs?
choices: The prayer's structure places God's glory and kingdom first, teaching the one praying to seek God's things before their own -- a deliberate order, not an arbitrary sequence
The order is arbitrary and carries no theological significance
Because early petitions are considered less important than later ones
Because Jesus originally taught the petitions in a different, reversed order
questions.correctAnswer: The prayer's structure places God's glory and kingdom first, teaching the one praying to seek God's things before their own -- a deliberate order, not an arbitrary sequence
questions.explanation: The Our Father's structure moves from petitions oriented to God (his name, his kingdom, his will) to petitions oriented to our needs (daily bread, forgiveness, deliverance) -- a deliberate ordering that shapes the one praying to seek God's things first, echoing Christ's own teaching to 'seek first the kingdom of God.'
questions.hint: Notice which petitions come first -- they aren't about us at all.

citations.quote: The first series of petitions carries us toward him, for his own sake: thy name, thy kingdom, thy will! It is characteristic of love to think first of the one whom we love.

questions.prompt: True or False: A monastery continuing to pray the Divine Office's night hour even when no visitors are present reflects the principle, per Sacrosanctum Concilium 84, that the Liturgy of the Hours sanctifies the course of the day itself, not merely serves as a performance for an audience.
questions.explanation: SC 84 describes the Liturgy of the Hours as extending the praise and thanksgiving of the Eucharist to sanctify the whole course of the day and night -- its value doesn't depend on an audience witnessing it, since its purpose is consecrating time itself to God, which a monastery continues whether or not anyone else is present.
questions.hint: The purpose named here is about time being consecrated, not about anyone watching.

citations.quote: The divine office is devised so that the whole course of the day and night is made holy by the praises of God.

questions.prompt: Match each experience or scenario to the correct traditional response.

pairs.left: 'Prayer feels dry and empty; I think it doesn't work anymore'
pairs.right: Spiritual dryness -- a real, common trial, not evidence prayer has failed

pairs.left: 'The Rosary is just vain repetition' (citing Matthew 6:7)
pairs.right: Matthew 6:7 condemns manipulative babbling, not attentive repeated prayer

pairs.left: 'Why ask God for things He already knows?'
pairs.right: Petition deepens a real relationship of trust, not supplying missing information

pairs.left: Someone wants to quit a daily holy hour purely from restless boredom with the good itself
pairs.right: Acedia, a form of spiritual sloth distinct from ordinary tiredness

questions.explanation: CCC 2725-2745's 'battle of prayer' names these as real, distinguishable trials -- each has its own traditional diagnosis and response, rather than a single generic answer of 'just try harder.'
questions.hint: One of these four names a specific vice, not just a difficult feeling.

citations.quote: More common in our own age is neither discouragement in the face of unanswered prayer nor presumption, but acedia.

questions.prompt: Someone prayed for years that a family member would recover, and they died. They ask whether God heard. What does the Catechism's teaching on filial trust actually say?
choices: Prayer is not a mechanism for obtaining outcomes; God answers as a Father, and the answer may not be the granting — which is not the same as not being heard
The prayer must have lacked sufficient faith
God always grants what is asked if the request is good
Unanswered prayer shows the person prayed incorrectly
questions.correctAnswer: Prayer is not a mechanism for obtaining outcomes; God answers as a Father, and the answer may not be the granting — which is not the same as not being heard
questions.explanation: The two wrong answers that blame the person do real damage and are commonly said. Christ's own prayer in Gethsemane was not granted in the form asked. Whether to say any of this to someone freshly bereaved is a separate question — often the answer is not yet.
questions.hint: Consider a prayer in Scripture that was heard and not granted.

questions.prompt: Someone says they have stopped praying because they no longer feel anything when they do. What is the most useful response?
choices: Feelings are not the measure; the Catechism treats dryness as the hour of sheer faith, and perseverance without consolation is prayer at its most costly
They should find a method that restores the feeling
The absence of feeling means God has withdrawn
They should wait until the desire returns before praying again
questions.correctAnswer: Feelings are not the measure; the Catechism treats dryness as the hour of sheer faith, and perseverance without consolation is prayer at its most costly
questions.explanation: Equating prayer with felt experience is the assumption underneath this, and it will eventually stop anyone praying. The last option is the most damaging in practice: waiting for desire to return usually means never returning at all.
questions.hint: Ask what is actually being measured when someone says prayer 'isn't working'.

questions.prompt: True or False: Praying at fixed times, even when one does not feel like it, is a lesser form of prayer than praying spontaneously when moved.
questions.explanation: False. The Catechism urges praying at regular hours precisely because feeling is unreliable, and a life ordered by set times of prayer is how 'pray always' becomes possible for someone with work and children. Spontaneity is good; depending on it alone means praying only when it is easy.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two survives a difficult month.

questions.prompt: Match each thing someone says about prayer to what actually answers it.

pairs.right: Asking changes the one asking, and God wills to be asked
Heard is not the same as granted; Gethsemane shows the difference
Dryness is the hour of faith, not evidence of absence
Turn back gently; distraction reveals attachment, not disqualification

questions.explanation: Each of these is usually said with real discouragement rather than as an argument. The answers matter, and the manner of giving them matters as much — delivered as corrections they confirm the person's suspicion that they were doing it wrong.
questions.hint: All four are more often confessions than objections.

questions.prompt: The Ignatian Examen is a short daily review. What is it chiefly for?
choices: Noticing where God was present and where you turned away during the day, so the pattern becomes visible over time
Producing a list of sins for confession
Assessing whether the day was productive
Deciding what to pray for tomorrow
questions.correctAnswer: Noticing where God was present and where you turned away during the day, so the pattern becomes visible over time
questions.explanation:
It is a review of a day for God's action in it, not an audit. Its power is cumulative: one Examen tells you little, a month of them shows you where you are consistently drawn and consistently defeated.

Try it tonight, five steps, ten minutes: ask for light; give thanks for two specific things; walk through the day noticing where you felt most and least alive; name one thing you regret and ask pardon; choose one concrete thing for tomorrow.
questions.hint: Ask what accumulates from doing it every night for a month.

questions.prompt: The previous level covered real, pastoral difficulties and doubts about prayer -- including the Ignatian Examen, a short, daily review, briefly named there. What is the Examen actually chiefly for?
choices: A brief, daily review noticing where God was present and where one fell short, bringing honest self-awareness into prayer
A real, lengthy theological study of the day's own events, requiring at least an hour of real, sustained analysis
The Examen actually has no real, practical purpose within a genuine, daily prayer life
A real, formal, liturgical rite that actually requires an ordained minister to actually lead it
questions.correctAnswer: A brief, daily review noticing where God was present and where one fell short, bringing honest self-awareness into prayer
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the Examen actually is -- a brief, daily review noticing where God was present and where one fell short, bringing real, honest self-awareness into prayer, as this topic's own earlier level already named.
questions.hint: Recall the previous level's own real, brief mention of the Examen as a short daily review.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Examen is a real, brief, daily review, not a real, lengthy, hour-long theological study.
questions.explanation: True, and this real, practical point matters -- the Examen's own real, brief, daily character is exactly what makes it a genuinely sustainable, further habit.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own real description of what the Examen actually is.

questions.prompt: How could someone actually begin the Examen as a real, structured daily habit, in genuinely practical, real terms?
choices: A few minutes at day's end asking two questions -- where was God present, where did I fall short -- ending in a brief prayer
Attempting a full, real, formal, hour-long theological analysis of the entire day, every single night
The Examen actually cannot be practiced without a real, trained spiritual director physically present
Waiting for a real, spontaneous urge to actually reflect, with no fixed, real, daily structure at all
questions.correctAnswer: A few minutes at day's end asking two questions -- where was God present, where did I fall short -- ending in a brief prayer
questions.explanation: This is a real, practical, achievable way to begin the Examen -- a few real minutes, two simple questions, ending in a brief prayer, matching this topic's own recurring, real pattern of starting small and sustainable.
questions.hint: Recall this topic's own recurring, real pattern for beginning any new, structured, daily habit.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Examen can actually be practiced in just a few real minutes, asking two simple questions, rather than requiring an hour-long, formal analysis.
questions.explanation: True, and this real, practical encouragement matters -- a few minutes and two simple questions is a genuinely achievable, sustainable way to actually begin.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own real, practical suggestion for beginning the Examen.

questions.prompt: Why does the Examen actually fit especially well right alongside real, pastoral honesty about prayer's own real difficulties, the previous level's own real subject?
choices: The Examen models the same honest self-awareness this topic has practiced throughout, naming difficulty rather than pretending all is fine
Because the Examen actually has no real, meaningful connection to pastoral honesty about prayer's own difficulties
Because the Examen actually requires denying any real, personal fault or difficulty ever occurred
Because the Examen actually replaces the need for any further, honest engagement with real, pastoral doubts
questions.correctAnswer: The Examen models the same honest self-awareness this topic has practiced throughout, naming difficulty rather than pretending all is fine
questions.explanation: This is a real, direct connection -- the Examen's own real, honest self-awareness fits exactly the same real pattern this topic has practiced throughout, naming difficulty honestly rather than pretending otherwise.
questions.hint: Consider what real, underlying habit the Examen actually shares with this topic's own earlier, pastoral honesty.

questions.prompt: True or False: The Examen's own real, honest self-awareness fits the same real pattern this topic has practiced throughout in naming prayer's own real difficulties honestly.
questions.explanation: True, and this real, shared pattern matters -- both the Examen and this topic's own earlier pastoral honesty practice naming real difficulty honestly, rather than pretending otherwise.
questions.hint: Consider what real, underlying habit the Examen actually shares with this topic's own earlier, pastoral honesty.

pairs.right: Both practice honest self-awareness, rather than pretending all is fine

pairs.left: Why this level's own approach matters
pairs.right: Turns a further, real, spiritual tool into an achievable, daily habit

questions.explanation: These four facts together turn the previous level's own real, brief mention of the Examen into an actual, achievable, daily practice.

questions.prompt: True or False: Having now covered the Examen as a further, real, structured daily habit, this topic's next level turns to the Trinity, kataphatic and apophatic prayer, and real guides for prayer.
questions.explanation: True. Having built this further, real, structured habit, this topic's next level turns to the Trinity, kataphatic and apophatic prayer, and the real, traditional guides for prayer.

Assuming the Examen should actually never be practiced as a genuine, daily habit
Replacing the previous level's own real content with an entirely unrelated, real practice

A complete repeat of this same level's material about the Examen
A jump ahead to named schools of spirituality, skipping over everything in between
A subject entirely unrelated to prayer or real, daily practice
questions.correctAnswer: The Trinity, kataphatic and apophatic prayer, and real guides for prayer
questions.explanation: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers -- moving from a further, daily habit to the Catechism's own real, deeper teaching on the Trinity and real guides for prayer.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: Per CCC 2664-2672, the Church addresses prayer to each Person of the Trinity in a specific way rather than interchangeably. To whom is Christian prayer, in its most proper Trinitarian structure, typically addressed, and through whom?
choices: To the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit
To the Holy Spirit alone, bypassing the Father and Son
To the Son alone, since only he became incarnate
Equally and interchangeably to whichever Person feels most fitting in the moment
questions.correctAnswer: To the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit
questions.explanation: CCC 2664 describes the Church's characteristic pattern of prayer as addressed to the Father, through Christ the mediator, in the power of the Holy Spirit -- a Trinitarian structure reflecting each Person's distinct role, not an arbitrary or interchangeable choice among three equally undifferentiated addressees.
questions.hint: This is the same structure found at the end of most liturgical prayers ('through Christ our Lord...').

citations.quote: There is no other way of Christian prayer than Christ... it has access to the Father only if we pray 'in the name' of Jesus.

questions.prompt: The Hail Mary places praise ('full of grace,' 'blessed art thou') before its petition ('pray for us sinners'). What does this structure reflect about the Church's understanding of Mary?
choices: Honoring Mary's unique grace and role first is fitting before asking for her intercession, reflecting her real dignity rather than treating her intercession as a mere transaction
The petition is considered more theologically important than the praise
The praise portion of the prayer was added centuries after the petition
The structure has no connection to any Marian doctrine
questions.correctAnswer: Honoring Mary's unique grace and role first is fitting before asking for her intercession, reflecting her real dignity rather than treating her intercession as a mere transaction
questions.explanation: Just as the Our Father orders God's glory before our needs, the Hail Mary orders praise of Mary's unique grace and role in salvation history before asking for her prayers -- a structure that reflects real Marian doctrine (her fullness of grace, her motherhood of the Redeemer) rather than an arbitrary sequence.
questions.hint: This mirrors the same 'God's things first' structure already seen in the Our Father.

citations.quote: By asking Mary to pray for us, we acknowledge ourselves to be poor sinners and we address ourselves to the 'Mother of Mercy,' the All-Holy One.

questions.prompt: CCC 2709 and 2717 distinguish kataphatic (image-using, imaginative) prayer from apophatic (imageless) prayer. A prayer practice that meditates on a Gospel scene, picturing its sights and sounds in the imagination, is best classified as which?
choices: Kataphatic
Apophatic
Neither, since imagination has no place in any legitimate Catholic prayer
Both equally, since the two terms are interchangeable
questions.explanation: Kataphatic prayer actively uses images, imagination, and concepts -- picturing a Gospel scene is a classic kataphatic approach, contrasted with apophatic prayer's movement beyond images and concepts toward a more direct, wordless resting in God's presence. Both are legitimate, complementary approaches within the Church's prayer tradition.
questions.hint: This term comes from the Greek for 'affirmative' or 'image-using,' as opposed to 'without images.'

citations.quote: Christian Tradition has retained three major expressions of prayer: vocal, meditative, and contemplative.

questions.prompt: True or False: The 'cloud of witnesses' in Hebrews 12:1 is connected by CCC 2683 to the Church's teaching that the saints in heaven can be asked to intercede for us.
questions.explanation: CCC 2683 draws on the image of the 'great cloud of witnesses' surrounding believers (Hebrews 12:1) as scriptural grounding for the Church's practice of asking the saints, who already share in God's glory, to intercede for those still on the earthly journey -- witnesses who are also companions in prayer, not merely spectators.
questions.hint: The image is witnesses surrounding and accompanying us, not just watching from a distance -- which is why they can be asked to pray for us.

citations.quote: Therefore, since we are surrounded by so great a cloud of witnesses, let us rid ourselves of every burden and sin that clings to us and persevere in running the race that lies before us.
The witnesses who have preceded us into the kingdom... share in the living tradition of prayer by the example of their lives, the transmission of their writings, and their prayer today.

questions.prompt: CCC 2685-2696 names several 'guides for prayer,' including the family, ordained ministers, religious life, and spiritual direction. Which of these is described as prayer's 'first school'?
choices: The Christian family
A monastery
A diocesan seminary
A retreat center
questions.explanation: CCC 2685 describes the Christian family as the 'domestic church' and the 'first school of prayer,' where children first learn to pray by seeing and joining their parents at prayer -- before any more formal guide (a priest, religious community, or spiritual director) enters the picture.
questions.hint: This 'school' has no classroom or formal curriculum -- it's simply where prayer is first modeled and learned.

citations.quote: The Christian family is the first place of education in prayer... the 'domestic church' where God's children learn to pray 'as the Church' and to persevere in prayer.

questions.prompt: Match each item to what CCC 2663-2696 teaches about it.

pairs.right: To the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit
Honors Mary's real dignity before asking her intercession
Actively uses images and imagination, e.g. picturing a Gospel scene

pairs.left: The Jesus Prayer (CCC 2667) and Western invocation of the Holy Name
pairs.right: Two forms answering the same need, shared inheritance rather than competing traditions

questions.explanation: CCC 2667 itself frames the Jesus Prayer as part of the Church's shared inheritance, not an exotic Eastern alternative to 'normal' Western prayer -- this level compares real methods without ranking one as more authentically Catholic than another.
questions.hint: The last pairing is explicit about not treating East and West as competing options.

citations.quote: The most usual formulation... 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us sinners'... combines the Christological hymn of Philippians 2:6-11 with the cry of the publican and the blind men begging for light.

questions.prompt: The Jesus Prayer — 'Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on me, a sinner' — is valued in the tradition chiefly because:
choices: It unites the invocation of the holy name with the humility of the tax collector, and can be prayed continually until it accompanies the breath
It is the shortest possible prayer
It replaces the need for liturgical prayer
It guarantees contemplative experience when repeated enough
questions.correctAnswer: It unites the invocation of the holy name with the humility of the tax collector, and can be prayed continually until it accompanies the breath
questions.explanation: The prayer joins two things: the holy Name, which the tradition holds is itself powerful, and the publican's plea, which keeps the one praying in the truth about himself. The last option is precisely the error to avoid — no repetition produces contemplation, which is given and not extracted.
questions.hint: Two Gospel elements are combined here: a name, and a sinner's words.

questions.prompt: True or False: Prayer addressed to the Holy Spirit is unusual in the tradition, since prayer is normally offered to the Father through the Son.
questions.explanation: False. The ordinary movement of liturgical prayer is to the Father through the Son in the Spirit, but the Church also prays to the Spirit directly — Veni Creator, Veni Sancte Spiritus — and the Catechism treats invoking him as the simplest and most direct way to enter prayer at all.
questions.hint: Recall two hymns sung at Pentecost and at confirmations.

questions.prompt: What is the danger in treating apophatic prayer as simply superior to kataphatic prayer?
choices: It mistakes a difference of mode for a scale of value, and can lead someone to abandon images before they are actually being drawn beyond them
Apophatic prayer is forbidden
Kataphatic prayer is only for beginners
Images are always obstacles to God
questions.correctAnswer: It mistakes a difference of mode for a scale of value, and can lead someone to abandon images before they are actually being drawn beyond them
questions.explanation: The Incarnation makes imageless prayer a strange thing to treat as automatically higher; God gave himself an image. Emptying the mind on purpose because one has read that the advanced do so is a technique, and the whole point of apophatic prayer is that it is not one.
questions.hint: Ask whether God's own self-revelation was imageless.

questions.prompt: Match each guide for prayer to what the Catechism says it provides.

pairs.right: The first place where prayer is learned, day by day
Formation of the faithful in the life of prayer
A form of life ordered wholly toward contemplation
Personal accompaniment in discernment

questions.explanation: The first is easy to overlook and hardest to substitute for. The Catechism calls the family the domestic church and the first school of prayer — nothing later fully replaces having seen adults pray.
questions.hint: One of these comes before any institution and is the hardest to replace.
